concept.name: Good-till-canceled order
concept.definition: An order that remains active until it is fully executed or explicitly canceled, persisting across trading days. In practice brokers and venues cap how long a GTC order can rest (commonly 30-90 days), so 'till canceled' is bounded by the firm's maximum order age.
concept.intuition: A GTC order is a standing instruction - set it once and it keeps working day after day until you pull it or it fills.
concept.mechanics: The unexecuted balance is carried forward each day by the broker/venue ('GT renewal' in FIX terms) and re-exposed to the market each session until filled, canceled, or aged out. Venues may adjust resting GTC orders for corporate actions such as stock splits.
concept.failure_modes: Forgotten GTC orders can fill weeks later into stale information - e.g., a GTC bid fills after bad news breaks but before the trader re-evaluates. Split or dividend adjustments can also leave the order at an unintended effective price.
concept.misconceptions: 'Good till canceled' does not mean good forever: brokers impose maximum durations, and exchanges may purge resting orders at their own discretion or on corporate actions.
concept.example: You leave a GTC limit order to sell 500 shares at $25; three weeks later the stock rallies to $25 and the order executes without you having re-entered it.
